1:
Balaam stops seeking enchantments, and the voices agree on the fact while differing on the man. Gill says no sacrifice could turn God's determined mind, much less a sorcery. Henry makes it a lesson, that it was to no purpose to deal with the devil for a curse when God was resolved to bless. Clarke will not let the word carry its usual weight, saying the meaning of nachash is not easily ascertained and that the plural here rendered enchantments probably means no more than the knowledge of future events, so that Balaam merely judged further inquiry unnecessary. Calvin is the least charitable: Balaam had been trying by various shifts to get the answer his paymaster wanted, as the wicked seek to propitiate God by delusive means, just as we soothe children by coaxing, and God for a time let him gloat upon his fallacious oracle; what happens now is not obedience but the closing of the last subterfuge, so that he dared not stir his foot.

That the Spirit of God should come on such a man is handled as a known category rather than a scandal. Ellicott notes the change of formula, that in the two former utterances Jehovah put a word in Balaam's mouth while here the Spirit came upon him, as of Saul and his messengers; and he adds Caiaphas as another instance of the Spirit's sovereign power through wicked men. Henry reaches for Saul too, and says Balaam spoke not his own sense but the language of the Spirit. Clarke observes only that Balaam had not expected this afflatus. Calvin is careful about the order: the sight of the camp did not itself suggest grounds for blessing, since Balaam felt no sincere goodwill; rather the Spirit prompted him to look that way so the impulse of prophecy might be stronger for having its object before his eyes, and then directed his tongue so extraordinarily that a divine majesty shone forth, as if he were transformed into a new man.

The word rendered open in whose eyes are open divides the catena five ways, the sharpest philological split in the chapter. Clarke argues flatly for shut, since the next verse uses a different word for opening, so the sense is the humble one of a man who once could not see even the angel in his path. Wesley glosses it who had his eyes shut, but now open, and Keil renders the man with closed eye. Henry keeps both, noting that many have their eyes open who have not their hearts open, and that such knowledge will only light them to hell. Ellicott declines to decide, observing that the form occurs nowhere else and that if the root is identified with its near neighbour it means to close, but that the next verse settles the sense either way, Balaam being in an ecstasy with the outer eye closed and the inner preternaturally opened. Calvin rejects both options as too poor and unnatural and proposes a third, that the eyes were hidden, because in their secret vision they have more than human power; he also passes on from Jarchi the conjecture that Balaam was blind in one eye.

On the word introducing the oracle, Ellicott and Keil agree that it is the standard prophetic formula for a divine saying, rarely used with a human name attached. On the preface itself Henry and Calvin part company. Henry hears pride and vain-glory in it, Balaam taking all the praise to himself and magnifying himself as one of the cabinet-council of heaven, where Paul speaks of his own visions with humility. Calvin allows that pride may have impelled the vaunt, but holds that the preface only proves him a true prophet speaking from revelation, that the boast was true as regarded this act, and that the Spirit itself probably prompted it, to demand more credit for the prophecy.
4:
The trance goes first, and Clarke takes it out of the text. There is no indication in the Hebrew that Balaam fell into a trance, he says: the words are added by our translators, the only word in the original signifying simply falling, perhaps by way of religious prostration. Ellicott renders it the same way but keeps the experience, noting the same physical effect on Saul, Ezekiel, Daniel and John, and that the word for opened is not the disputed word of the preceding verse but one frequently used of divine communications. Keil translates falling down and with opened eyes. Wesley alone keeps both, calling it a vision properly so called because Balaam was awake, and the trance an ecstasy, fainting and falling to the ground, as the prophets used to do.

The next word divides them because it is the same word twice. Clarke observes that the aloes of the sixth verse are spelt exactly as the tents of the fifth, the root meaning to spread or branch out, which fits tents on the ground and wide-branched trees equally well; he settles for a tree whose leaves grow at the top, so that a forest at a distance might resemble an encampment, while admitting the species cannot be ascertained. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by another route, that although the word often means tabernacles it must here be trees, since what follows speaks of cedars. Both read which the Lord hath planted as growth independent of cultivation, and Wesley says it in two words, nature, not art. On the cedars Ellicott is exegetical, distinguishing those whose roots reach running water from the sort that spend their strength on branches. Clarke instead assembles three eyewitnesses of Lebanon, the longest digression in the chapter.

The buckets produce the chapter's most concrete description. Clarke explains the machine: a tall pole by the well as fulcrum to a long lever, a bucket on the short arm, notches in the long arm for a man to climb up and lower it, then walk back until his weight raises it; and the seed in many waters alludes to rice, whose ground must be flooded, all applied by an elegant and chaste metaphor to the procreation of a numerous posterity. Ellicott and Keil prefer water shall flow from his buckets, personifying the nation as a man carrying two pails, water being the leading source of blessing in the East; Keil notes the dual form and dismisses sowing corn as very feeble. Gill and Wesley spiritualise it, Gill making the rain a figure of the grace that waters the churches, Wesley extending it to the word and the Spirit and at last to eternal life, whose contemplation made Balaam desire to die the death of the righteous.

Agag is taken by nearly all as a title, not a man. Ellicott calls it a nomen dignitatis like Pharaoh and Abimelech and refers the prophecy to the kingdom to come rather than a particular king; Wesley adds Caesar and infers Amalek's power from their bold attempt on so numerous a people. Calvin rejects the conjecture that Saul is meant and reaches further, holding that Balaam, however little aware, embraced the time of David and so predicted things only accomplished in Christ. Clarke stands apart with a textual proposal, that with the Septuagint a small change gives than Gog for than Agag, making the promise dominion over all God's enemies. The closing lion is conquest settled rather than begun, Gill referring the couching to the armies in the plains of Moab and Wesley to Israel resting in a conquered land, while Ellicott corrects the second lion to a lioness. Calvin ends on the blessing, that God counts as done to himself whatever Israel receives; and he meets the objection that Balaam blessed and went unrewarded by denying he deserved reward, having been forcibly drawn where he was unwilling to go.
10:
Balak's rage is the breaking of a long restraint. Gill says he had borne much and long but could bear no longer. Ellicott notes only that smiting the hands was a token of strong feeling, scorn or indignation or despair. Calvin makes it a rule about the wicked, that when their lusts are pressed under the yoke they are carried into passion; Balak smites his hands because he can no longer restrain himself, and is galled that Balaam bore witness to the blessing openly, since nothing is more galling to kings than to see private men regard their presence without alarm. Henry hears the charge in it, that Balaam had put upon Balak the basest affront and cheat imaginable, having by the building of altars made him expect a curse.

On the taunt that the Lord had kept Balaam back from honour, four hear sarcasm and one will not. Clarke calls it a bitter and impious sarcasm: hadst thou cursed this people I would have promoted thee, but thou hast preferred Jehovah, and what will he do for thee now? Wesley reads it the same way, seek thy recompence from him and not from me; Keil calls the irony unmistakable. Ellicott alone leaves the other door open, allowing that Balak may by now have been convinced of the supernatural influence on Balaam. Calvin splits it as none of them do: what Balak says is true, God having kept Balaam back from honour, but he says it impiously, laying on God the blame for a promise he himself is breaking.

Balaam's defence is accepted as true and rejected as insincere. Henry allows it a very good excuse, since God restrained him from saying what he would and constrained him to say what he would not, Balak having had fair notice of the check. Keil observes that he is only repeating what he told the messengers at the outset, and Ellicott notes that the commandment of the Lord is in Hebrew the mouth of the Lord, as at that refusal. Calvin grants the truth and attacks the spirit: Balaam excuses himself with servility, grieving for his lost reward, and for all his grand declaiming on God's supremacy signifies that he acted under compulsion. Calvin then reads three words closely. The word of the Lord means not the decree only but the dictation Balaam would have preferred to alter; do refers to his tongue, since he was hired for no manual act but only to injure by speech; and of mine own heart is set against the Spirit's revelation, impostors being said to speak out of their own heart when they use God's name to cover their inventions.

What Balaam offers at parting is the chapter's second dispute. Henry takes the sinister reading outright: unable to get leave to curse, Balaam puts Balak in a way of getting help from the devil to tempt, counselling him privately to entice Israel to idolatry; and Henry seals it with the tag that one who cannot move heaven solicits hell. Ellicott refuses to find that here: the word generally means to advise, and the announcement of Israel's supremacy was itself advice, implying the folly of opposition; and though the Targum of Palestine inserts the seduction here, no reference to it is in the verse. Keil reads it benignly, as advice on what attitude Balak should take if Israel is to bring a blessing. Calvin reports the sinister view and a milder one, that Balaam advised Balak to rest quiet since Israel's prosperity would not harm Moab in his lifetime; he himself takes it as simply to teach. Ellicott and Keil agree that what follows is exclusively future and falls into four parts marked by the repeated parable; and Calvin adds the sting, that having heard only Israel blessed, Balak must now hear his own nation's ruin, which is the reward of those who strive against God.
15:
The preface returns with one clause added, and that clause is what the expositors seize. Calvin says Balaam renews it to gain authority for weightier matter, and that although the titles were not proclaimed without ambition, God ratified by them what he meant to deliver, since this worthless man, whose doctrine would else have been contemptible, needed divine marks upon him. Henry answers each boast: many hear the words of God who neither heed them nor hear God in them; a man may be full of the knowledge of God and yet utterly destitute of the grace of God, receiving the truth in the light of it and remaining a stranger to the love of it; and he saw the vision but was not changed into that image. Clarke presses his earlier point again, charging the Targum with the false paraphrase of open that most versions followed.

Whom Balaam sees is settled by argument. Ellicott says it cannot be Israel, whose armies stood before his bodily eyes, so the object must be one beheld with the mind; and the verb is the prophetic past, there hath come forth a Star, a tense denoting certainty. Clarke reads it as a denial of presence: the person prophesied of does not exist among these Israelites. Keil refers the suffixes to the star named later. Calvin alone hesitates, and only over a detail: the pronoun designates someone not yet named, and he will not contend whether head or body is meant. Gill, Wesley and Henry take the seeing to be personal and future, Wesley saying Balaam shall see him in his own person as every eye shall at the judgment, Henry adding that he shall see him not as Job did but afar off, as the rich man saw Abraham.

Whether the Star is David or the Messiah is answered by nearly everyone with both. Clarke reports Maimonides dividing the verse clause by clause, David and Messiah alternately, and calls it a perfect hit. Henry gives the same as type and antitype. Ellicott assembles the external evidence: both Targums read a King and a Messiah, Ibn Ezra reads David while reporting that many read Messiah, the pretender under Adrian took the name son of a star from this text, and the Magi's words look back to it. Henry supplies a mechanism, Balaam being of the east, where the tradition may have been kept. Calvin agrees David is in it but refuses to let him be enough: the glory of his kingdom was neither lasting nor wide, impaired by the revolt of the ten tribes and finally extinguished.

The children of Sheth divide them four ways, and the verb divides them further. Henry takes it universally, of all men descended from Seth the son of Adam, the other lines having perished in the deluge, so all must either be governed by Christ's golden sceptre or dashed by his iron rod. Calvin says that reading violently wrests the text, since the parallel clause names Edom with Mount Seir by way of explanation and the two sentences are identically formed, so none but the Moabites can be meant; and he offers two accounts of the title, that they claimed the descent to cover the incest their nation sprang from, or, as he prefers, that like the Amalekites they boasted of the antiquity of their race, the name ironically reproving that vain-glory. Wesley makes it neither, guessing at some then eminent but now unknown place or prince in Moab, and remarking how many famous names have wholly perished. Ellicott and Keil drop the proper name for sons of tumult or of confusion, Ellicott adding a conjecture that the verb be repointed to give the crown of the head. Clarke declines to choose and lays six renderings side by side: shall waste, shall prey on, shall rule over, shall shake, shall put a yoke on, shall unwall.
18:
Edom and Seir come first, and the grammar is agreed before the history. Ellicott and Keil both take his enemies as standing in apposition to Edom and Seir rather than depending on Seir, so the two names are themselves the enemies who become a possession; and both add that Edom names the people, Seir the country. On fulfilment they divide by degree. Clarke splits the verse, giving Edom to David and Seir to the king Messiah; Ellicott says the primary accomplishment came under David and the ultimate in Christ Gill runs the history furthest, through the Maccabees to the subjugation of the Idumaeans by Hyrcanus, when they became one people with the Jews, which he says is reported not only by Josephus but by the heathen Strabo; and he then reads the whole spiritually of the calling of the Gentiles.

On the ruler and the remnant the argument turns on a preposition. Ellicott renders it he shall destroy the remnant from the cities, taking the singular collectively of Edom's cities and not of Jerusalem, and Keil agrees, calling the destruction of a remnant out of the holy city forced and unsustainable by the parallelism. Wesley reaches the same sense without the philology: the ruler will not merely beat his enemies in the field but pursue them to their holds.

Clarke then dissents from almost everyone about the Star. He will not have it that the star which guided the wise men is meant here, nor that Peter's day star or the Revelation's morning star refers to this prophecy; and he denies that the false Christ under Adrian was appealing to it, on a neat ground: a son of a star is not the Star, so the pretender must first have shown his supposed ancestor had reigned. He offers instead only that sun, moon and stars were always titles of royalty among the Asiatics.

Amalek called the first of the nations produces a flat contradiction. Clarke takes it as the most ancient and powerful state then in Balaam's view. Keil denies exactly that, naming Knobel and answering that a Bedouin tribe descended from a grandson of Esau was surpassed by many nations in age and power, so the title must mean the first heathen nation to attack Israel. Calvin takes the opposite side as flatly, calling the first-to-attack reading poor and unsatisfactory and finding instead an indirect rebuke of Amalekite pride, since they claimed precedence for their antiquity, as if they had been created together with the sun and moon. Ellicott weighs both, noting that the word more often denotes priority in time and the answering word for latter end supports it, while the earlier mention of Amalekite kings favours rank; both may be intended. Wesley gives both without deciding, adding that the victory was an earnest and firstfruit of a harvest of victories.

The Kenites divide four against one. Wesley makes them Jethro's kindred, but only the part mingled with the Amalekites and Midianites. Gill likewise refuses Jethro's family, against Aben Ezra and Jarchi, since those were not a people by themselves but encamped with Israel and went into Canaan; he allows only a people of the same stock dwelling near Amalek. Clarke, following Dodd, identifies Kenites and Midianites as the same or confederate tribes, and notes that Saul had no commission against them, they having by then been wasted, though by what means does not appear. Calvin says simply that by the Kenites he understands the Midianites, and calls it altogether unreasonable to refer the name to Jethro's descendants, since barely forty years had passed and Jethro's was one small family, where a celebrated people is meant. Keil stands against all four, arguing from usage that the Old Testament knows no Kenites but those who went to Canaan with Hobab, so that the distinction between Canaanitish and Midianitish Kenites has no ground and the identification with Midian is unfounded.
22:
The clause about Asshur is taken historically by most, grammatically by Calvin. Gill says the Kenites, fortified as they were, should gradually waste away, being few already in Saul's time; Clarke assumes the Assyrians and Babylonians carried them off with the ten tribes and Judah, confirmed by Kenites appearing among the Jews after the return; Wesley traces the same deportations and glosses Kain as a transposition of letters, or the name of some place or person whose memory is now utterly lost. Calvin refuses the usual construction, calling it harsh and unnatural to apply the clause to the Kenites at all, reporting that most refer it to Israel but divide between an affirmative and an interrogative rendering, and preferring the interrogative, how long shall Asshur hold thee captive, the point being that the prosperity just promised should be mixed with heavy affliction. Keil hears in the cry who shall live the fearfulness of the coming judgment, which went deep to the seer's heart because it would fall on the sons of his own people.

Chittim sets off a geographical inquiry which four conduct separately and settle alike. Clarke reports that some think the Romans and others the Macedonians under Alexander, that Calmet strongly contends for Macedonia, and concludes from Josephus, who settles their posterity in Cilicia, Macedonia, Cyprus and Italy, that both may be meant. Ellicott traces them from Phoenicia to Cyprus, where they founded Citium, takes the name to cover the Mediterranean coasts generally, and notes that the Vulgate renders it triremes from Italy and identifies the Kittim with the Romans in Daniel. Wesley walks the migration from lesser Asia through the Aegean islands to Macedonia and Italy, and says the name means sometimes one, sometimes the other, here both. Calvin and Gill arrive by the same unusual route, both pointing to the Roman embassy that halted Antiochus, Gill putting it as Romans in Grecian ships.

Eber divides them three ways. Wesley takes it of the Hebrews, the chief and flower of Eber's children, and is careful that the he also who perishes is not they, since all Israel shall be saved, but the afflicter, the Grecian and Roman power, and he closes with the neatest sentence in the chapter, that Balaam, instead of cursing the church, curses Amalek its first and Rome its last enemy. Ellicott keeps the Hebrews but widens the term to all the children of Eber, conjecturing that Asshur may stand for the Eastern Shemites and Eber for the Western. Clarke excludes the Hebrews altogether, deriving the name from the verb to pass over and taking it of the peoples beyond the Euphrates.

Whether Balaam ever got home is left open with care. Keil insists the Hebrew says only that he turned towards his place, not that he reached it, so that whether he did must be settled from other evidence. Ellicott says he probably set out meaning to go home, but the sequel shows he stayed among the Midianites and perished with them, though Gill allows he may have reached Mesopotamia and come back. Calvin ignores the itinerary and reads the parting as commendation of God's grace, which dissipates the counsels of the wicked like clouds, the enemies departing in dishonour without their purpose. Clarke then closes the chapter with seventeen numbered propositions arguing that the badness of this man's character has been very far overrated: that he knew and worshipped the true God, was a true prophet, used no spells or necromancy, sought God's will by the means God prescribed, told Balak faithfully all God said, and refused rewards of the most extensive kind, so that covetousness is almost the only blot on him; that the fatal counsel may have been only advice to seek alliance by marriage with a people Moab could not conquer; and that the blame rests ultimately on Israel's readiness to cast off godliness at so slight an invitation.
